newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Concern raised over Bank Melbourne fee hike.
newsitem.headline: Concern raised over Bank Melbourne fee hike.

text.p: Bank of Melbourne Ltd's hike in its fee charges, bringing its fee structure closer in line with its suitor Westpac Banking Corp, is reducing consumer choices, Australian Consumer Association (ACA) said on Monday.

ACA policy manger Mara Bun said the Bank of Melbourne raised its annual fees for its standard deposit account to A$73.32 from A$6.12 just a day after Westpac lodged its agreed A$1.435 billion takeover of the Victorian-based bank.
Bun said the Bank of Melbourne previously had some of the lowest bank fees in the country. Westpac charges about A$113.12 per year for its equivalent deposit account.
The Westpac-Bank of Melbourne deal is also facing scrutiny from the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX) over the timing of the announcement.
The Bank of Mebourne sought a share trading halt on Wednesday ahead of Thursday's merger annoucement.

Before the trading halt, the bank's shares jumped 65 cents to A$8.80. Bank of Melbourne's shares have slipped off their high of A$9.75, Westpac offer price, to under A$9.40 as investor fears that regulatory and government approval was not assured.
Bank of Melbourne shares closed nine cents lower to A$9.38, while Westpac shares ended one cent lower at A$6.82.

The government is expected to release the Wallis report into Australia's financial system this week and has warned Westpac that it was taking a risk by launching a bid before its policy response had been issued.
Coopers and Lybrand banking and finance partner Jeremy Pooley said regulatory approval was not certain.
"This will really test its commitment to the one regional bank policy," Pooley told Reuters.
The ACCC announced the one regional bank policy when it approved Westpac's purchase of Challenge Bank in late 1995.
Bun said since Westpac's takeover of the Perth-based Challenge bank the banking fees of the two groups had narrowed.

"Price pressure comes generally comes from competition it rarely comes consistently from big incumbent players and if we eliminate competition there is real risk that the kind of dynamics that we have in place may be profit over good value and that just does not make the market function well," Bun said.
Andrew Willink, managing director of banking products research group Cannex, said a Westpac takeover of the Bank of Melbourne would not necessarily limit competition.

"Nationally there are 460 financial institutions that ranges from the building society and credit unions and mortgage orginators. The choice from the consumer point of view is huge," Willink told Reuters.
"In some areas there should be some rationalisation as many consumers are confused with the vast number of choices available," Willink said.
